rationale: A wins because it does the adult thing: it leads with the caveat instead of trying to outrun it. "Peloton posts its first profitable quarter in three years — on adjusted EBITDA, not net income" is the real story shape; B's "The company everyone wrote off" imports a consensus the update did not prove and makes the angle smell like a comeback victory lap. B has useful instincts, but A is cleaner, more defensible, and less likely to get a founder embarrassed on the first reporter call.
gaps_in_A: "Peloton is selling bikes by the month now — the hardware company is becoming a subscription company" slightly overstates the shift; Peloton already has a subscription business, so the sharper version is rental/access changing hardware economics.
"The cost program is credited in this quarter's turn" implies attribution the supplied facts do not explicitly prove; A correctly asks for proof, but the line should stay conditional.

The exec angle asks for the CEO's name and background, which is right, but it still calls this an "exec-spotlight" before knowing whether that person is available or interesting enough to carry a profile.
gaps_in_B: "The company everyone wrote off" is unsupported swagger. The update does not prove everyone wrote Peloton off, and this kind of contrarian throat-clearing is how decent facts get dressed up as CNBC cosplay.

"The prevailing belief is that pandemic-era connected-fitness winners are in permanent decline" invents a market consensus not supplied in the update. Maybe true, maybe not; either way, it needs evidence before it becomes the spine of an angle.
"Record-low churn is doing more for Peloton than any new bike" is a claim B cannot substantiate from the facts. There is no comparison to new bikes, product launches, or causality.

"cost-cutting playbook that got Peloton to its first profitable quarter" overclaims causation. The update says costs were cut and adjusted EBITDA/free cash flow turned positive; it does not prove the cuts caused the quarter.
